name: GitLab
license: Open core: MIT for everything outside the `ee/` directory (the Community Edition); `ee/` is under the proprietary GitLab Enterprise Edition license and needs a paid tier
summary: A Git forge sold as one application for the whole software lifecycle, from issues and merge requests to built-in CI/CD, packages and security scanning, that you can use on GitLab.com or run yourself.
intro: GitLab is a Ruby on Rails application served by Puma, with Sidekiq running background jobs from a Redis queue. It doesn’t touch repositories directly: every Git operation goes through Gitaly, a separate service written in Go, built so large installations no longer need repositories on shared NFS. GitLab Shell handles `git` over SSH, Workhorse, a reverse proxy, takes load off Puma, and PostgreSQL, the only supported database, holds users, issues, merge requests and permissions. A self-managed single server starts at 8 vCPUs and 16 GB of memory.

What sets it apart is scope. Issues and boards, merge requests (GitLab’s name for pull requests), CI/CD from a `.gitlab-ci.yml` file, a package and container registry, security scanners and deployment tracking share one data model and one permission system, so a pipeline’s results, a vulnerability and the issue it fixes all appear on the merge request. Jobs run on GitLab Runner, an agent you install on your own machines or use hosted on GitLab.com. GitLab ships a new version on the third Thursday of every month and a major version every May; 19.5 came out on October 15, 2026.

The code is open core. Everything outside the `ee/` directory is MIT and builds the free Community Edition; the `ee/` features are proprietary and unlocked by the Premium ($29 per user a month) and Ultimate tiers. You can use it on GitLab.com, run it yourself, or rent GitLab Dedicated, a single-tenant instance GitLab runs for you. GitLab Inc. has been listed on Nasdaq since 2021, reported $955.2 million of revenue in its fiscal year to January 31, 2026, and says GitLab has more than 50 million registered users.
strengths: One product for the whole loop: code, review, CI/CD, packages and security scanning without wiring separate tools together
You can self-host all of it, CI included, from the free MIT-licensed Community Edition up to Ultimate
Open about how it works: the source code, the company handbook and even outage postmortems are public
A predictable cadence: a release every month on a fixed day, and a major version once a year in May
limits: Heavy to run yourself: a single server starts at 8 vCPUs and 16 GB of memory, and needs PostgreSQL and Redis alongside
Team controls cost money: required approval rules, code owner approvals and merge trains are Premium or Ultimate only
The free tier on GitLab.com is small: 5 users per private top-level group, 400 compute minutes a month and 10 GiB of storage
Security fixes go only to the latest three monthly releases, so a self-managed instance must be upgraded every few months

snippet.title: A merge request from the terminal with the GitLab CLI
source: git commit -am "Extend login session timeout to 30 minutes"
# pushes the branch and opens a merge request against the default branch
glab mr approve 235          # a reviewer approves
glab mr merge 235 --squash   # auto-merges once the running pipeline succeeds

story: Dmitriy Zaporozhets needed a good tool for his team to collaborate on code. Working from a house in Ukraine that had no running water, he decided the missing collaboration tool was the bigger problem, and with Valeriy Sizov he started GitLab: the first commit is dated October 8, 2011. Sid Sijbrandij found it in 2012, thought it natural that a tool for programmers should be open source, and started GitLab.com. In November 2012 Zaporozhets wrote the first version of GitLab CI.

In 2013 large organizations running GitLab asked for features they needed, Zaporozhets said he wanted to work on GitLab full time, and he and Sijbrandij introduced the paid Enterprise Edition. The company was incorporated in 2014 and went through Y Combinator in early 2015 with nine people. It stayed all-remote, and wrote down how it works in a public handbook.

That openness was tested on January 31, 2017, when an engineer wiped the production database directory on the wrong server and the backups turned out not to work. GitLab.com was down for about 18 hours and lost about six hours of database changes, and the team live-streamed the recovery on YouTube. GitLab Inc. went public on Nasdaq on October 14, 2021, priced at $77 a share and describing itself as “The DevOps platform, a single application.”

choices.choice: One application instead of a toolchain
choices.why: GitLab added CI in 2012 and then planning, packages, security and deployment to the same product, so teams share one data model, one interface and one set of permissions instead of integrating separate tools. It is how GitLab described itself when it went public.

choices.choice: Open core, split by who buys the feature
choices.why: GitLab Inc. earns almost all its revenue from paid tiers. Its stewardship promises say a feature whose likely buyer is an individual contributor goes into the MIT-licensed core, one aimed at managers or executives is proprietary, open features are never moved to a paid tier, and features land in both editions at the same time.

GitLab’s source code and company handbook are public. After the 2017 database outage it kept its recovery notes in a public document, live-streamed the work to about 5,000 viewers, and published a detailed postmortem.

timeline.text: Dmitriy Zaporozhets and Valeriy Sizov start GitLab in Ukraine (first commit October 8)
Sid Sijbrandij starts GitLab.com; the first GitLab CI (November)
GitLab Enterprise Edition introduced for larger organizations
Graduates from Y Combinator in March with nine people
GitLab.com database outage, recovered on a live stream (January 31)
$955.2 million revenue in fiscal 2026 (March); GitLab 19.5 released October 15
